content: A headache is a condition characterized by pain localized in the head. In some cases, pain in the neck or upper back may also be perceived as a headache. Headaches are among the most common complaints of localized pain. The first documented classification system resembling modern headache classifications was published by Thomas Willis in De Cephalalgia in 1672. Later, in 1787, Christian Baur categorized headaches into two main types: idiopathic (primary headaches) and symptomatic (secondary headaches), defining a total of 84 categories. The brain itself is not sensitive to pain because it lacks pain-sensitive nerve fibers. However, several areas of the head can experience pain, including a network of nerves that extend over the scalp and certain nerves in the face, mouth, and throat. The meninges (the protective layers surrounding the brain) and blood vessels are capable of perceiving pain. Headaches often arise from traction or irritation of the meninges and blood vessels. Additionally, the muscles of the head can also be sensitive to pain. The majority of headaches are benign and self-limiting. Common causes include tension, neck pain, migraines, eye strain, dehydration, low blood sugar, and sinusitis. Chronic headaches are often multifactorial in origin. Rarely, headaches may result from life-threatening conditions such as meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral aneurysms, extremely high blood pressure, or brain tumors. When a headache occurs in conjunction with a head injury, the cause is usually apparent. A significant proportion of headaches in females are associated with fluctuating estrogen levels during the menstrual cycle, which can occur before, during, or even mid-cycle. The prognosis of a headache depends on its underlying cause. Blood tests may assist in narrowing down the differential diagnosis of headaches, but they are rarely definitive for specific headache types. Computed tomography (CT) scans of the brain or sinuses are commonly performed, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and sinuses is used in specific clinical scenarios. Headaches can often be effectively treated with medical therapies, such as analgesics. In some cases, advanced treatments, including the use of implanted electrodes, may be employed. Certain types of headaches, such as migraines, may benefit from preventative treatment strategies.
